A 

NEW 

VENTURE 

FOR 

THE 

BLIND 


By Paul C . O’Neill 


A blaze of sound and colour is 
perhaps the best description of the 
GNIB Adjustment Training and Holi¬ 
day Centre which completed its first 
season last September. You saw it 
from Highway 69 as you drove along 
Lake Joseph from MacTier. Then, 
you heard it — the sounds of happy 
people enjoying a vacation. Once 
afoot on this eighteen-acre site, you 
found that this blending of summer 


sound and the warm gay colour was 
everywhere. It was on the five sandy 
beaches where squeals and laughter 
mingled with the splashing of the 
wax es and the whispering of the wind. 
It was in the gurgling of the brook 
which flowed past the recreation 
lounge. Behind the buildings, sound 
and colour blended again as blind and 
sighted joined in quoits, shufTleboard 
and other outdoor games. 

Through the season some three hun¬ 
dred blind campers and their escorts 
had a holiday at the centre. The 
number was something of an achieve¬ 
ment since the centre was not operat¬ 
ing until late July. In fact, the new 
facilities created several records. The 
first was in the construction phase. 
Planning and construction were com¬ 
pleted, grounds landscaped and open 
air games installed in just over a year. 
A new system was introduced for 
financing the capital fund of $400,000. 
The Ontario Government made a 
special grant of $50,000. The Lion’s 
Club of District A, Ontario, agreed to 
subscribe $350,000 over the next three 
to five years. Individuals donated some 
$20,000. These arrangements avoided 
a special building fund campaign and 
permitted the erection of the facilities 
without delay. 

Eight residence units, with bath¬ 
rooms and screened verandahs, accom¬ 
modate 114 persons a day. A large 
recreation-lounge serves for evening 
affairs and rainy-day activities. An 
airy dining-hall provides full-course 
meals. Craft and hobby rooms offer 
spacious quarters where trained blind 
instructors hold classes in handskills 
and adjustment-training arts. 

Outside, guide rails lend safety and 
security to the wooded parts of the 
property, along the hundred-foot dock, 
and up the hill to the summer house, 
now known as Kenwood Point. A 


46 


Canadian Camping 


plaque records the dedication to the 
memory of the late H. Kenneth Wood, 
former chairman CN1B Ontario Divis¬ 
ion Board of Management and CNIB 
associate for more than twenty-five 
years. 

From the opening day July 21st, 
to closing in mid-September, CNIB 
Lake Joseph provided an active out¬ 
door programme for those who wished 
it. They swam, rowed, hiked through 
the bush, threw horseshoes and bowled 
on the lawn or played shuffleboard. 
Others relaxed on the verandah or 
lazed on the sands. At night they 
danced, played bingo, took part in 
talent nights and watched movies while 
the sighted acted as narrators. As they 
left for home, blind and sighted alike 
were loud in praise of the summer 
centre. Some of them even signed up 
for 1962. 

For the first time in Canada, blind 
persons have a summer centre built 
to their needs, arranged for their 
safety and planed for their comfort. 

Blind Canadians have always taken 
an active part in outdoor life. From 
time to time CNIB rented facilities 
for small groups of sightless campers. 
The most successful of these was the 
Lions Club Camp at Ancastcr, Ontario 
where CNIB provided two ten-day 
holiday periods for twelve years. Al¬ 
together more than 2,000 blind persons 
enjoyed this programme. 

Ancaster was not designed for the 
blind. It had numerous hazards, but 
demonstrated that blind people were 
anxious to spend a part of the summer 
in the country and that they could 
handle a properly supervised outdoor 
life. 

At Lake Joseph sunshine, fresh air, 
good food and freedom of movement 
will rebuild the health of the newly- 


blind, as they take full advantage of 
the outdoor readjustment programme. 

Rehabilitation means adjustment to 
blindness. It requires many CNIB 
services and training by experts to 
restore confidence and self-reliance to 
a newly-blind person — training to 
walk well with a white cane, training 
in home-making for a blind housewife, 
training on-the-job for a blind worker. 

Recreation also is a major part of 
adjustment-training, since it offers the 
blind person a chance to enjoy himself 
with blind companions while he learns. 

Young blind children and their 
parents will spend a period at CNIB 
Lake Joseph. Under expert super¬ 
vision they will be encouraged to climb 
the Jungle Gym, use the swing, teeter- 
totters and other playground equip¬ 
ment installed for their development. 
A safe, shallow beach strip is marked 
off for junior bathers. Teenagers will 
receive swimming lessons devised for 
touch-type instruction. They will be 
encouraged to join in competitive 
games and to take part in an advanced 
junior programme prepared for them. 

Some of the special equipment you 
may see at the summer centre includes: 

*—Pedal boats and nursery play¬ 
ground apparatus for the use of 
blind children. 

—Guard rails on the hundred foot 
dock. 

—Water markers to provide maxi¬ 
mum safety for blind swimmers. 

—Water safety trained personnel 
will be on duty at all times. 

The first centre of its kind in Can¬ 
ada, CNIB Lake Joseph put a new' 
dimension into the Institute’s service 
programme and stands as a pilot pro¬ 
ject for a new Canada-wide service 
to the sightless. 

—• 


Toronto , Canada , February 1962 


47 



Sermons 

^inber 

Cljc H>un 

An address to older boys at Camp Pine 
Crest, by Robert Me Knight — Wilderness 
Trip Leader. 


“It is often depressing to me to see 
how the youth of today has degener¬ 
ated from its once high ideals into its 
present state. I can recall the days 
when youth was proud and strong, 
steadfast in its goals, and devoted in 
its duties. Now it is mean and strives 
without aim. It is sad”. 

Much as this passage sounds like 
something which we might read in 
any newspaper or journal today, this 
selection was actually written by the 
famed Greek philosopher Aristotle, in 
the year 293 B.C. It seems, then, 
that just as Aristotle was concerned 
about the youth of Athens, so every 
age worries about its young people. 
There are, of course, things peculiar to 
today’s adolescents that were never 
heard of in ancient Greece. I very much 
doubt whether Fabian, Rock and 
Roll, portable radios, go-karts, hula- 
hoops, Disneyland, pizza and Huckle¬ 
berry Hound, were known in those 
days. I also doubt whether the number 
one song in Grecian teenage circles 
would be, as it is right now in 
Toronto, the very profound “Who put 
the Bomp in the Bomp Bomp Bomp.” 

Certainly youth is a confusing period 
of life as most of you know. One 
moment you are regarded as an adult, 


“Now come on Johnny and act grown 
up”. The next moment you are re¬ 
garded as a child, “No Johnny, you’re 
too young to do that!” I suppose we 
often get the feeling that we would 
like to be past this difficult period of 
time and into adulthood. And yet 
youth holds so much for us that to 
think this way is to miss a very 
important aspect of life. For youth is 
a glorious time of life, a time when 
there are things to be done, new skills 
to be learned, new experiences to be 
lived. Most of all, it is a time when 
we have it within our power to shape 
our future and to realize those goals 
and aspirations for which we strive. 
How often have you heard it said, 
“If I only had my life to live over 
again”. This is impossible of course, 
and therefore, we must make the best 
of it the first time through. 

The value and importance of youth 
can be illustrated by the way in which 
man seeks for it in today’s world. 
Millions of dollars are spent each year 
on products such as Metrecal, Man 
Tan, hair dye and facial creams, be¬ 
cause they presumably work towards 
a more youthful appearance. History 
records man’s search for youth. I am 
sure most of you have studied about 
the explorer Balboa who sought for 
the fountain of youth. Many writers 
have devoted much time and space to 
a discussion of youth—William Words¬ 
worth, John Keats, and Joseph Con¬ 
rad. Conrad writes “O Youth! The 
strength of it, the faith of it, the 
imagination of it. Youth that so 
quickly passes, unseen, in a sigh, in a 
flash together with the romance of 
illusions”. 

The strength of youth. Surely all 
of us have thrilled to the feeling of 
physical power and well-being after 
having successfully conquered the 
waves of Georgian Bay, or carried a 
pack over a long portage, or run a 
great distance. It is this challenge, this 


48 


Canadian Camping 



pitting of human strength against 
natural forces that represents one as¬ 
pect of the spirit of youth. Often on 
canoe trips I allow a camper to carry 
a canoe over a portage. Often the 
camper has to make several stops to 
catch his breath and rest his shoulders. 
And yet, it is very seldom that the 
camper asks me to carry the canoe the 
rest of the way. For though he is 
tired, portaging the canoe is to him 
a sort of test or challenge which he 
feels can only be won by completing 
the portage. Youth craves adventures 
and struggles. Let us experience and 
enjoy them while we are young. 

Conrad also mentions the illusion of 
youth and in a sense it is an unreal 
world. The child and adolescent are 
not concerned about the major prob¬ 
lems of the world such as the popula¬ 
tion explosion, but rather about more 
personal and vital things such as 
whether the girl next door still likes 
him, or whether he will make the team 
next fall. 

Finally, there is the romance of 
youth. Life has to it a certain magic 
which it has at no other period of 
time. This is why men often revisit 
their boyhood haunts and think of the 
activities and adventures that filled 
their boyhood days. 

Conrad is right, youth does pass 
simply because it is inevitable that we 
must all grow older. St. Paul said, 
“When I was a child I spoke as a 
child, I thought as a child, I under¬ 
stood as a child; but when I became a 
man I put away childish things.” And 
so must we all, for childish acts have 
no place in our lives beyond our 
immediate childhood. They do, how¬ 
ever, have a very real place in our 
childhood. A child should be childish. 
He is supposed to be; he was created 
to have a score of years to grow up. 
Yet paradoxically our society is always 


attempting to shorten the span that 
nature intended. It is so pleased if 
he can talk at one, though he has 
sixty-nine years more to carry on con¬ 
versations. It is thrilled if he can read 
at five, forgetting that he will have six 
and a half more decades to be greeted 
each morning with the headlines. But 
while he can read all his life, whenever 
again will he have the thrill of keep¬ 
ing a frog in the bathtub or kicking 
leaves, or making a secret tree house. 

You will notice that our educational 
system is set up with the constant 
idea of “getting ahead”, just like a 
motorist who rushes to his destination 
without enjoying the scenery he passes, 
the boy becomes a man without ever 
experiencing the joys of childhood. Let 
us not let this happen to us. Let us 
take full opportunity of our youth and 
live it fully and completely. 

I can recall one of my English 
teachers drawing a distinction between 
the words “childish” and “child-like”. 
While it is inevitable that we must put 
away childish things as we grow older, 
child-like qualities are a different 
matter. I am speaking of the qualities 
of inquisitiveness, frankness, and intel¬ 
lectual and emotional honesty that 
adults should strive to maintain. Too 
often as we grow older the question 
becomes “What will people think of 
me”, rather than “What do we think 
of ourselves”. A perfectly innocent 
statement by a child such as “Mommy, 

I have to go to the bathroom” is 
immediately hushed by the parents if 
there is any company present. People 
conform to one dull standard and life 
becomes a drag. There is a nine-to-five 
job day in, day out, followed by long 
evenings of television. Life becomes 
little more than a worry about disease, 
taxation, inflation, fall-out and com¬ 
munism. Certainly this type of man 
has desires and aspirations, but usually 
they consist of no more than a desire 


Toronto , Canada , February 1962 


49 


to keep up with the Joneses, and to 
drive a nice, big, shiny car so every¬ 
one can see what a wonderful success 
he has made of life. It is invariably 
this type of man that we read about in 
the newspaper dying at the age of 51 
leaving some great fortune, but never¬ 
theless having literally worked himself 
to death. 

It is the man who stays out of this 
mad rat race for wealth that really 
has a chance to live. Life holds for 
him values and truths higher than 
mere physical wealths. There is always 
something new and interesting to hold 
his attention. He delves into the fas¬ 
cination of nature and in doing so 
maintains his child-like inquisitiveness 
and interest in life. When Franklin 
Delano Roosevelt died in 1944, it was 
generally felt that his wife having 
served her husband and country well, 
would settle down into a semi-retire¬ 
ment. Instead Eleanor Roosevelt be¬ 
came a goodwill ambassador for the 
United States and generally an out¬ 
standing humanitarian. She is indeed 
an ageless woman for she has learned 


the secret of enduring youth — an 
interest in life and a concern for others. 

Let us thrill to our physical strength 
and endurance in our youth. Here at 
camp we have the opportunity to run, 
to dive and to swim, as we please. 
And as we grow older while we may 
lose some of our physical vitality, let 
us never lose our appreciation of things 
beautiful, sunsets and skies, trees and 
rocks, rivers and lakes. Most of all, 
let us live life to the hilt constantly 
exploring new fields, remaining in¬ 
quisitive and learning more about the 
fascinating world in which we live. 
Only by this means can we come closer 
to nature which holds the secret of 
our very existence and purpose. Only 
by this means can we maintain within 
ourselves the spirit of youth. For the 
English novelist wrote, “What a large 
volume of adventures may be grasped 
within this little span of life by him 
who interests his heart in everything 
and who having eyes to see what time 
and chance are perpetually holding 
out to him as he journeyeth on his 
way, he misses nothing he can fairly 
lay his hands on”.

NEWS FROM THE PROVINCES 

Congratulations to the Nova Scotia Camping Association for 
the fine Newsletter that is being sent to all representatives of Nova 
Scotian camps. It is an excellent publication chock full of informa¬ 
tion and ideas. 

With their permission, perhaps we could quote from it from 
time to time. 

If any provincial association would like to receive a copy of 
this newsletter, they should address their request to Mr. C. A. 
Griffith, Nova Scotia Camping Association, P.O. Box 578, Halifax, 
Nova Scotia. 

If any other provincial associations send out newsletters, we 
would be pleased to receive a copy so that we may keep abreast 
of provincial news.

Canadian Camping 



Here's how one camp I rains its leaders 



by DON GROFF, 

Director of Youth and Camping, 
Kit chener-Wdterloo Y.M.C.A., 
and Director of Camp Wabanaki. 


LEADERSHIP DEVELOPEMENT 


Some years ago the Kitchener- 
Waterloo Y.M.C.A. Camping Depart¬ 
ment in an eff ort to meet the leadership 
needs of its two resident boys’ camps 
and one resident girls’ camp, embarked 
upon a scheme which we now feel we 
would like to share in some greater 
detail with our colleagues in the camp¬ 
ing field. Like camps everywhere we 
face the problem of continually finding 
leadership for our camping programme. 
For the following reasons this scheme 
was devised, and experimented with 
until the present format was adopted. 

1. to provide a stimulus and chal¬ 
lenge for leadership training for our 
camper personnel; 

2. to orient leadership candidates to 
camping philosophy and to train them 
in the basic programme skills, which 
they will require in future staff 1 per¬ 
formance ; 

3. to provide an enthusiastic spark 
for camp activity which can be pro¬ 
duced through the carefully guided 
group experience of a more imaginative 
and senior age level of camper: 


4. to provide additional programming 
and incentive for senior campers. 

The course has been in operation 
now at our Ki-Wa-Y campsite, (thir¬ 
teen miles outside of the Twin Cities) 
for the past ten years, and at our 
Wabanaki Beausoleil Island site (both 
boys’ and girls’ camps) for the past 
six years. 

The programme is divided into a 
two year progressive training plan. The 
first year we designate as the Junior 
Leader phase and second year partici¬ 
pants are referred to as Counsellors- 
in-Training. In the Junior Leader 
Course, ten to fourteen first or second 
year high school students are registered 
as full paying campers in a special 
section of the camp whose programme 
follows a rigid training schedule 
throughout the entire duration of the 
camp period. Candidates are selected 
from senior campers of previous sea¬ 
sons and also from first season appli¬ 
cants to the camps. The second year, 
or phase, of the course enrolls auto¬ 
matically those graduates who have 
successfully completed the Junior 


Toronto, Canada, February 1962 


51 


Leader Course of the year previous. 
They return to camp as apprentice 
staff members and are assigned to 
camper cabin groups, or to special 
departments as assistant leaders. 

During the first year, Junior Leaders 
registered in our training course follow 
a curriculum divided into four major 
categories. Within each of these, they 
proceed along a course of study which 
involves demonstrations, lectures and 
training techniques. They learn leader¬ 
ship skills such as first-aid; receiving 
instruction to the equivalent of the 
Junior St. John’s Ambulance Course. 
In life-saving they will proceed either 
to their Junior Y.M.C.A. Certificate 
or its equivalent. For those who have 
previously completed their life-saving 
requirements they may well continue 
on to Master Swimmer standing or 
some other advanced stage of swim¬ 
ming skill. Story telling, song leading, 
dramatics (and their use in the camp 
programme); and out-trip leadership 
are included among the other leader¬ 
ship skills taught during the course. 

The course also encompasses leader¬ 
ship techniques, including those of 
cabin leadership—the household duties 
which pertain to keeping campers 
healthy and happy at camp. Teaching 
methods and instructional techniques 
are also taught. Council fire and camp¬ 
fire planning, the conduct of religious 
programmes such as cabin devotions, 
the planning of church services, etc., 
and games leadership are all a part of 
this year of their training. 

Much of the training in leadership 
techniques is done through demonstra¬ 
tion whereby candidates in the course 
will be taught a certain lesson and 
then in turn will be required to teach 
it to each other or to campers they 
may have in their charge for that day. 
All the camp programme skills are 
also included here in this first year of 


leadership training. For those who have 
not been in attendance at the camp 
for any great length of time, or in some 
cases not at all previously, an effort 
is made to assist them to achieve a 
minimum standard in the various camp 
skills. Sports; handicrafts; campcraft; 
nature lore; and all of the aquatic skills 
are included in this phase of their 
training. 

The last category involves leadership 
fundamentals, and these are very 
basically outlined and presented in such 
sessions as understanding oneself, un¬ 
derstanding the camp whom he will 
lead and developing a personal belief 
and philosophy of life. 

Complete in a camper cabin setting 
themselves, candidates rotate the coun¬ 
sellor role in a counsellor-of-the-day 
system which provides a guided ex¬ 
perience in the daily routine of cabin 
leadership. Programme planning and 
teaching techniques are also taught 
through projects by which Junior 
Leaders Course candidates will provide 
programme for specific times during 
the daily activities of the regular 
camper sections in camp. 

Counsellor-In-Training Course 

The second phase of the course, that 
is, the counsellor-in-training year, is 
divided again into three main parts,— 
the first of which is in service training. 
Because of their involvement with the 
campers and their setting in the camp 
itself, the counseilors-in-training are 
provided with opportunities to share 
behaviour problems and ‘‘ideas that 
work”, either during regular coaching 
interviews with the training staff or 
by means of periodic lecture-discussion 
sessions often held around a late 
evening campfire with marshmallows 
included.

ONTARIO CAMPING ASSOCIATION ANNUAL CONVENTION 


March 23 and 24 — King Edward Hotel — Toronto, Ontario 
Guest Speakers: 

Mr. Fay Welch, State University College of Forestry, Syracuse, New 
York. Director of Tanager Lodge, a camp for boys and girls in the 
northern Adirondacks. Mr. Welch will take two session at the con¬ 
ference. His topic will be “CONSERVING OUR NATURAL AND 
HUMAN RESOURCES.” 

Professor Charles Hendry, School of Social Work, University of Toronto. 
Professor Hendry is to give the first of the Taylor Statten Memorial 
Lectures. His topic will be “TOWARD A NEW UNDERSTANDING 
OF LEADERSHIP.” Professor Hendry is well known in camping 
circles. He was associated with Taylor Statten for many years and is 
the author of several books including “Camping and Character”, “A 
New Understanding of Leadership” and “A Professional Approach to 
Group Education.”

ASSOCIATION DES CAMPS DU QUEBEC CONVENTION 

March 22, 23, 24, — Sheraton Mount Royal Hotel — Montreal, Que. 


The theme this year is “CAMP—SUMMER EDUCATION” 

Guest Speaker:— 

Mr. Sam Kadison, Director Camp Modin, Canaan, Maine. Mr. Kadison 
is also Camp Consultant for the Jewish Welfare Board of the United 
States. He will be guest speaker on Thursday and Friday evenings as 
well as taking a session for counsellors on Saturday.

ANNUAL MEETING OF THE CANADIAN CAMPING ASSOCIATION 

March 22, 6:00 p.m. — Mount Royal Hotel 


Toronto, Canada , February 1962 


53 



iV. B. Pouiter, 

Owner and General Manager, 

Powter f s Camp 

describes camping of 

60 HORS 060 


In June 1902 a group of 50 boys 
from the Montreal area under the 
leadership of the late C. B. Powter 
arrived on the shores of Lac St. 
Joseph near Ste. Agathe des Monts, 
some 60 miles north of Montreal. 
Here they established Camp “Sans 
Egal” (“Without Equal’’) the first 
private camp in Quebec and one of 
the first in Canada. 

— Background — 

It was here that C.B. began to 
put into practice some of the theories 
he had developed concerning the 
teaching of sportsmanship, self reliance 
and responsibility towards and by the 
group, and above all imparting a love 
of life in the outdoors. He firmly be¬ 
lieved that personal leadership and ex¬ 
ample were the keys of teaching 
physical skills and social behaviour 
patterns. He could be kind, patient 
and considerate yet he was a disciplin¬ 
arian of the old order demanding and 
getting instant obedience when the 
occasion warranted. 

As a young man he was an accom¬ 
plished sailor, paddler, and mountain 
climber. In the early 1890’s he decided 
on a career of physical education and 
took a course at the Y.M.C.A. College 
at Springfield, Mass. On his return 
to Montreal he joined the “Y” staff 
and became captain of the first basket¬ 
ball team to play in Canada. He also 
directed the Y.M.C.A. camp at Lac St. 
Joseph which had been founded in 
1893 but “Y” work and particularly 


their style of camping were not to his 
liking and he became Instructor of 
Physical Training at the High School 
of Montreal. After several seasons of 
camping with a mixed group of young 
adults from Montreal he was con¬ 
vinced that camping offered a wealth 
of new experiences to boys of high 
school age. 

— The Early Days — 

Since I was only seven months old 
at the time I am afraid that my 
account of those early years is only 
hearsay backed by perusal of old photo 
albums and diaries. Apart from moving 
the camp from its original site to the 
then little known Lac Archambault 
region some 26 miles north of Ste. 
Agathe, the early years were pretty 
much of the same pattern. 

In the interests of brevity the first 
20 years of the camp are presented as 
a composite. They might be called 
the horse-and-buggy years for the 
camp was isolated from the railroad 
by 5 to 7 hours riding in metal-tired, 
practically springless buckboards, over 
a primitive road. Then came the 
automobile, and with it, the visitors 
and parents to force the camp out of 
its pioneer ways. At the same time 
the age levels were progressively 
lowered and the seniors and leaders of 
16 to 19 disappeared. The 1920’s then 
saw the turn toward the more highly 
organized staff and programmes which 
have led to the development of present 
day camping. 


54 


Canadian Camping 



— Organization — 

By today’s standards the staff organi¬ 
zation of the early years was sketchy. 
C.B. had one or two paid Assistants 
but they weren’t paid very much as 
the camp fee was only $1.00 a day 
including transportation. Of course 
there was the camp Chef, usually from 
a lumber camp, beloved but some¬ 
times feared by the boys. The main 
problem was to keep him sober during 
the season. There were a few hilarious 
episodes I can still remember of the 
cook walking or stepping off the wharf 
in search of his misplaced (?) boat, or 
the time he slept in the ice house 
thinking he was in his own cabin— 
both the meals and the chef were cold 
that day. 

Below the Assistant level everyone 
paid the regular camp fee. Each tent 
had six occupants and they were of 
mixed ages. The senior boy in age or 
experience was called the Leader and 
was held fully responsible for the boys 
in his tent group. At the beginning 
of camp he was assigned his tent 
number and in turn each leader chose 
his secondj third, fourth, fifth, and 
sixth man, usually in descending order 
of age down to the minimum of 9 
years. Care was exercised in striking 
a balance of age and aptitude in the 
various tents so that real competition 
could exist between them. Like coun¬ 
sellors of today, Leaders and Seconds 
had certain special privileges in return 
for their extra responsibilities. Since 
there were no staff instructors it fell 
upon the Leader to teach his tent 
members the various sport skills other¬ 
wise he fell behind in the inter-tent 
competitions. 

The tents themselves were the con¬ 
ventional “A” style 9 x 12 ft. with 3 
foot walls. There was a small platform 
in front and also one runing down one 
side on which the rough-wood hinged- 
top clothes lockers were positioned. 


A two-rail rack hung from the ridge 
pole on which all placed pyjamas and 
extra clothes. The boys slept on fine- 
cut balsam and spruce boughs, each 
“bunk” separated from the other by a 
6 or 7 inch board. The Leader occu¬ 
pied the bunk farthest from the 
opening while poor number six had the 
flap bunk, probably on the theory 
that in a severe storm his bed was 
likely to be more than a little damp 
anyway. 

— Around Camp — 

To keep things tidy there was an 
inspection every morning at 9 a.m. 
Marks were reduced by the presence 
of paper, matches, glass, tin cans etc. 
all along the front of the tent line 
and 20 to 30 feet behind. Blankets 
were folded and hung on racks or 
during rainy spells the order came for 
“beds made and rolled”. No wet 
clothes or bathing trunks were per¬ 
mitted in the tents. 

Weekly inspection was held Sunday 
morning and as C.B. had an eagle eye 
and the points counted so heavily, in 
competition extra time was spent in 
sprucing up. Blankets were folded 
neatly in the bunks. On the racks 
each boy had to have a dry change 
of clothing in the following precise 
order “ “Stockings, pants, shirt and 
pyjamas.” His clean (?) towel had 
to be folded neatly on top of his locker 
and in prescribed order — “toothbrush, 
toothpaste, soap, brush, comb and 
knife.” On the platform in front of 
the locker were a pair of dry shoes 
flanking his axe or hatchet which had 
to be sharp and free of nicks. 

At the call of “Inspection” all work 
ceased even if not finished and the 
boys sat quietly on the front platform 
with the Leader and Second on the 
left. At the approach of C.B. '• they 
rose smartly to attention and doffed 
their hats. “All present tent 3” would 


Taranto, Canada, February 1962 


55 



be answered by “All present and 
accounted for Sir”. This system stem¬ 
med from the military but it induced 
smartness and teamwork in the whole 
tent group. 

— Programme And Safety — 

Although there was no organized 
daily programme C.B. insisted that 
everyone keep busy. Loafing was not 
tolerated and anyone caught was given 
some menial task to perform. Keeping 
a watchful eye on the culprit was one 
of the duties of the Officer of the Day, 
usually one of the Leaders or Seconds. 
He was also responsible for discipline 
in the Clubhouse and the waterfront. 
He called “Swim” at 11 a.m. and 4 
p.m. He made sure a patrol boat and 
crew were in position at swim time. 
He saw that all boats and canoes 
were bailed and in working order and 
had his “Rescue Boat” and its crew 
available at all times in case of an 
upset dinghy or other emergency. He 
was equipped with binoculars and a 
megaphone and sat on the clubhouse 
gallery overlooking the waterfront. 
Anyone leaving the camp boundaries 
had to check in with the Officer-of-the- 
day who kept a record of who was 
where and in what. 

There were more “Do’s” in the 
Safety Rules than “Don’ts”. C.B. 
worked on the premise that you didn’t 
keep a knife from a boy in case he 
cut himself but rather you showed him 
how to use it properly. He carried that 
through in all camp activities. A series 
of incentives made the boys want to 
improve their skills. For instance, non¬ 
swimmers were limited to rowboats 
and were allowed in canoes only up 
to “one-half-paddle-depth”. They were 
limited to land hikes or the odd over¬ 
night trip by rowboat. If, however, 
they could swim a hundred yards and 
could demonstrate some proficiency in 
and on the water all of those activities 
were opened up to them. 


— Canoe Trips — 

Of all the camp activities canoe 
tripping was certainly the major one 
just as it is today. In the early days 
the surrounding area was unmapped 
and practically unknown. It was still 
being lumbered but the cutting crews 
kept to watercourses where the logs 
could be floated thus there were many 
areas of virgin woods which were sel¬ 
dom visited even by trappers. Apart 
from two free runs of about 10 miles 
each, a canoe had to be portaged more 
than it was paddled. The terrain is 
typical of the Laurentians consisting of 
a mass of rounded hills and ridges up 
to 3200 feet above sea level with the 
lower areas at least 1000 feet. Civiliza¬ 
tion ceased four miles north of camp 
and from then on it was canoe and 
trail. 

Canoe trips at first followed the main 
watercourses and the lumberman’s 
rough winter roads. Soon, however, 
exploratory side trips were made from 
previously established campsites. These 
followed up small streams particularly 
if the water was warm, because that 
usually meant it came from a lake or 
lakes. Many side trips were mountain 
climbs where, perched on the top of a 
tall tree, new lakes and valleys could 
be seen and a rough route planned for 
reaching them. Gradually over the 
years successive trips from the camp 
cut trails to practically every lake 
within a radius of 25 miles West, 
North and East. 

For six years triangulation measure¬ 
ments were made from various moun¬ 
tain peaks and by 1915 the first camp 
map was drawn up on a scale of 2 
miles to the inch, showing mountain 
peaks, lakes and portages. The camp 
also adopted a three blaze signal for 
its trails. These were put on all trail- 
side trees for the first hundred or so 
yards and at each point where loghauls 
or other trails intersected. It is amazing 


56 


Canadian Camping 


how accurate the map was. When an 
aerial survey was completed in 1927 
there were very few lakes to be added 
and that original map plus a few 
modifications is still the most accurate 
and most helpful for trippers. Practi¬ 
cally every camp in the area uses it 
for their out trips and Fire Rangers 
are using the trails cut so many years 
ago by the campers from Powter’s. 

— Practical Tripping — 

In some respects the boys travelled 
much lighter than they do today. Each 
had a blanket roll or “horse-collar” 
containing a dry change of clothing. 
These also were used as neck pads 
for portaging. There were only two 
tumpline packs for each 10 boys which 
held the tent fly and most of the food. 
This consisted of bread, porridge, rice, 
raisins, bacon or salt pork, cornmeal 
for pancake mix, molasses, corned beef, 
beans, butter, sugar, coffee, tea and 
condensed milk, but not all at the 
same meal of course. 

Because the country was so little 
travelled food could be cached any¬ 
where on the way out and picked up 
on the return journey. But that meant 
good timing especially on round trips 
where two canoes travelled the same 
circuit from opposite ends leaving food 
for each other on the way. The one 
big advantage was that trips could 
always count on fish. Most of the 
surrounding lakes teemed with trout, 
but a few draining into the Devils 
River country had pike. Practically 
everyone took tackle of some kind with 
them and sufficient catches could be 
made to supplement the other rations 
at least for breakfast and supper. Any¬ 
one who has savoured a succulent fresh 
caught brook trout, rolled in cornmeal 
and cooked in bacon fat over a bed of 
gleaming coals knows that the boys 
ate well notwithstanding any deficiency 
in the carried grub. 


Tripping, however was certainly 
rough going. Since the boys from 
Powter’s were practically the only ones 
travelling the bush in summer they 
had to keep the trails open and cut 
new ones to the unknown areas. Every¬ 
one in the party then, carried an axe, 
a hatchet or a machette. These latter 
were not the heavy short models of 
today but were actually Jamaican cut¬ 
lasses, larger, lighter and slightly 
curved. 

C.B. had learned to use them as a 
boy during his 10 years residence in 
the Red Hills of Jamaica and they 
proved to be one of the most useful 
tools in the woods. They were ideal 
for small shrubs and trees up to 3 
inch diameter. They could take off a 
considerable number of small branches 
with one slash, they were excellent for 
blazing trees and could substitute as 
a large knife or even a can opener. 
They are still being used today but it 
is difficult to find models of the same 
weight, balance and quality of steel. 

— Exploring New Country — 

The reader may wonder why 
campers worked so hard to open up the 
country. First it was because C.B. was 
a natural woodsman and a trip with 
him was always interesting. He was 
never in so much hurry that he 
wouldn’t stop and point out some land 
or water feature. He taught them the 
various kinds of birds and trees and 
their uses. He showed them the tracks 
of wild animals and often if he could 
keep the boys quiet on the trail they 
could catch a glimpse of the animal 
itself. He showed them how to light 
fires in rainy weather, how to cook 
and how to choose and prepare a 
campsite. Above all he taught them 
how to buck bush to a mountain or 
lake and how to break branches thus 
leaving a back-trail. He instilled in 

turn to page 67 


Toronto, Canada , February 1962 


57 



We must do something about 


WATER POLLUTION 

before it’s too late! 

(from a Royal Bank letter) 


Disease-carrying water 

Dr. Gustave Prevost, head of the 
biological bureau of the Quebec Fish 
and Game Department, said in Feb¬ 
ruary: “People have become so used 
to living with polluted water that they 
have become indifferent to the problem 
and accept it as a necessary evil.” 

Everybody relies upon the undoubted 
fact that science has conquered the 
great water-borne diseases, but the 
reality remains that the source of the 
diseases — pollution — has not been 
stopped. 

The protective wall built by science 
keeps epidemics from ravaging our 
cities, but in small ways pollution is 
slipping through the wall. Vague in¬ 
testinal symptoms put us to bed for a 
few days, and we learn on getting back 
to the office or factory that others, too, 
have been laid up. 

It is no wonder such things happen. 
How can the grey and greasy scummy 
water we sec along the shore, or the 
filthy conglomerate we find on the 
bottom of the stream, be turned with¬ 
out fail into sparkling and pure tap 
water to fill our drinking glass 

It is time we started to take stern 
preventive measures. Consider the fact 
that it was sixty years after scientists 
had discovered the link between cholera 
and sewage-polluted drinking water 
before methods for the purification of 
water began to bring typhoid, endemic 
diarrhea, and dysentry under control. 


It will take us a long time to restore 
our streams by cleaning the water we 
return to them. 

Pesticides 

Insects are man’s greatest competitor 
for the food he eats. Our survival 
demands that we control them 
effectively. 

However, this does not demand that 
we spray-kill everything that crawls, 
flies, bites or bores. In too many cases 
we have also killed birds, animals, fish 
and bees, and we have poisoned the 
streams from which we drink, and the 
fruit and vegetables we eat. 

Pesticides, wisely applied, have done 
much to improve agriculture and give 
us better health, but their use involves 
a calculated risk and demands wide¬ 
spread education. Farmers have a 
definite responsibility for safe use of 
chemicals, and those who instruct them 
in the use of chemicals have even 
greater responsibility. 

Unknown ten years ago, there are 
now on the market well over 12,500 
brand name products and more than 
200 basic control compounds. These, 
while fulfilling their function on land, 
may enter our water supply by direct 
application to the water surface, by 
drifting on. to the water surface from 
treated fields, or by seepage from the 
watershed. This offers death to fish, 
to birds, to aquatic animals, and, it 
may be, danger to man. As a speaker 
said at the National Conference on 


58 


Canadian Camping 



Water Pollution in Washington in 
December 1960: “We are running an 
unnecessary risk when we just blithely 
go ahead and use these things because 
we have not died yet.” The report of 
this conference is available from the 
Superintendent of Documents, U.S. 
Government Printing Office, Washing¬ 
ton, D.G., for $2.25. 

We need pest control, but it is im¬ 
perative that it be guided by responsible 
and objective leadership and that other 
interests be appropriately co-ordinated 
with the objectives of control. 

As a start, public education, and 
education on the county agricultural 
level, should demonstrate to users of 
sprays and insecticides of all sorts that 
the material is extremely toxic to fish 
life and must be excluded from our 
waters. A strong declaration on the 
national level and by the provincial 
governments would have a beneficial 
effect in the public interest. 

There is proof aplenty of the need. 
Several years ago severe mortality oc¬ 
curred among coho fry, trout and steel- 
head yearlings when a western province 
forest was sprayed to control the black¬ 
headed bud worm. Ninety-one per cent 
of young salmon were killed in an 
eastern province when a forest was 
sprayed against spruce budworm, and 
aquatic insects wiped out at that time 
had not re-established themselves even 
sixteen months later. 

Wildlife and recreation 

Turning to non-human sufferers, we 
find that pollution vitally affects birds 
and fish and other wildlife. It threatens 
the existence of aquatic vegetation, the 
small aquatic insects, the mollusks and 
the crustaceans on which our water- 
fowl, game fish and water-loving mam¬ 
mals depend. 

There have been heavy losses of 
waterfowl to pollution on the Great 
Lakes and in their connecting waters. 
On one occasion some ten thousand 
ducks, mostly the scarce canvasbacks 


and redheads, were destroyed on the 
Detroit River by the release of un¬ 
treated sewage. 

In the United States, the area of fish 
and wildlife habitat rendered unpro¬ 
ductive every year by pollution is 
greater than that created by all public 
agencies conducting fish and wildlife 
restoration programmes. 

Interest in the relationship of fish 
population to water pollution is not by 
any means restricted to academic re¬ 
search. The supreme interest in the 
subject is expressed by the angler who 
discovers a stream full of dead fish, and 
by the commercial fisherman who finds 
his fishing area barren. 

These people — those who respect 
and value fish and fishing for food or 
recreation — are increasingly demand¬ 
ing that authorities give effect to at 
least the minimum guarantees. All the 
replenishment of fishing grounds by 
hatchery stock will be futile if the en¬ 
vironment of the fish is not right. 

There are three types of waste affect¬ 
ing fish: organic wastes causing oxygen 
depletion; wastes that are directly toxic; 
and non-organic wastes which cause 
some mechanical change either to the 
fish directly or to their habitat. For 
example, sawdust has all three types: 
it demands much oxygen, it exudes 
toxic substances, and it can directly 
injure gill filaments through mechani¬ 
cal abrasion. In addition, sawdust 
settles to the bottom of the stream and 
is capable of burying spawning gravels 
and bottom organisms. Soil erosion also 
contributes to sediment pollution, dam¬ 
aging the stream habitat for all the 
more desirable fish. Thousands of miles 
of otherwise fine fishing water have 
been taken out of production because 
of the acid damage from coal mines or 
the poisonous effluent from industrial 
plants. 

Oil pollution has its place in the 
roster of practices damaging fish.

from page 59 

Sooner or later ships, particularly those 
using our inland waterways, must be so 
designed that the wastes can be 
pumped ashore for treatment or treated 
on board. 

Sewage disposal 

The state of affairs involving pollu¬ 
tion of our rivers by sew f age got out of 
control before the magnitude of the 
problem was realized, and we have not 
been aggressive enough with our treat¬ 
ment programmes to catch up, let alone 
get ahead of the grim condition. 

The methods of sewage treatment 
have now been developed to a high 
degree of efficiency. Primary treatment 
removes some thirty-five per cent of 
the pollutants by screening and sedi¬ 
mentation. Secondary treatment re¬ 
moves, by such means as trickling filters 
or the activated sludge process, the 
wastes that are in solution or in colloi¬ 
dal suspension. As a result of primary 
and secondary^ treatments, around 
ninety per cent of the organic matter 
originally present can be removed be¬ 
fore the effluent is discharged. 

Why is this treatment not universal 
in Canada? It is safe to say that there 
are tw'o reasons: the need has not been 
appreciated, and the cost is not relished. 
The first excuse can be eliminated by 
education: the second is not so serious 
when the facts are obtained. The cost, 
spread out over thirty to fifty years, 
said Dr. Prevost, would be less than a 
cent a day per person. There are, he 
said, 350 such plants in Ontario. While 
there were about forty sewage treat¬ 
ment plants in Quebec, only about 
three or four of them treated sewage 
completely before flushing it into rivers 
and streams. 

Whatever the cost, authorities across 
Canada are showing signs of shrugging 
off the inertia that has held back action. 

The Prime Minister declared in 
November 1960 that pollution of Can- 


60 


Canadian Camping 





ada’s rivers and streams is “one of 
the most potentially dangerous threats 
to our whole economy.” In March it 
was announced that the federal govern¬ 
ment has voted $100 million to help, 
and is prepared to lend up to 66 per 
cent of the construction costs and to 
make a gift of 25 per cent of this 
amount to any municipality that 
finishes its work before March 31. 1963. 

A 16-rnan national committee of 
prominent engineers and scientists is at 
work studying the use, conservation and 
pollution control of Canada’s water 
resources, with a final report due at 
the end of this year. This committee 
was set up by the Engineering Institute 
of Canada and the Canadian Institute 
on Sewage and Sanitation. 

Ontario is putting its shoulder to 
the job of eliminating pollution of its 
streams at a cost the Premier says will 
be six times that of the St. Lawrence 
Seaway. 

In Quebec, briefs were presented to 
the government in March telling the 
seriousness of the situation in this 
province and emphasizing the urgency 
of remedying it. In May, the govern¬ 
ment decided on appointment of a per¬ 
manent water purification board having 
extensive investigating and regulatory 
power, and offered financial aid to 
municipalities in the form of a one- 
sixth subsidy. In June, Dr. Gustave 
Prevost was appointed chairman. 

Responsibility 

Where does the responsibility ulti¬ 
mately lie? The answer is plain and 
simple: every city and town, every in¬ 
dustry, is responsible for cleaning up 
the pollution it creates. Stream sanita¬ 
tion is a co-operative responsibility, 
involving everyone along the banks. 

Cities and towns and industries need 
to call upon the professional and tech¬ 
nical people who have knowledge of 
these matters. In turn, the people who 
plan the remedy must take into con¬ 
sideration all the users of water. 


Pure tap water and clean water for 
industrial processes are essential; so is 
the wildlife of our streams and lakes. 
Society suffers if one segment of our 
resource base is managed alone without 
consideration of all others. 

After competent engineers collect the 
data and make recommendations, then 
the force of public opinion enters. The 
lag between the decision to do some¬ 
thing effective and the start of work 
on the projects must not be long. 

The antipollution movement offers 
an outstanding opportunity for country¬ 
wide co-ordination, dynamic leadership 
and effective action. 

Pollution control fits into the pur¬ 
poses of nearly all civic organizations, 
business, conservation, service and in¬ 
dustrial. They can all assist, and not 
only by passing resolutions. They can 
use their own interest, whether boating 
or swimming, hunting or fishing, irrigat¬ 
ing or draining, or just enjoying nature, 
to press for action. 

Positive pollution control 

Pollution control in the past has been 
mostly corrective; in the future it must 
be preventive. Gross pollution is an 
offence to human decency, and it can 
be corrected only by positive methods 
and controls. 

Science and technology have pro¬ 
vided the tools, and are capable of 
providing better tools as we need them. 
All we have to do is get at the job 
in dead earnest. 

We should do so in a spirit of ma¬ 
turity of judgment, and not in panic 
actions which will provide half-measure 
solutions. 

Then, within our lifetime, we may 
see our ruined streams so rehabilitated 
that they no longer offend the nose and 
eve; we may enjoy our beaches; we 
may see birds and fish and small 
creatures return for our enjoyment — 
all this, if we sincerely desire to meet 
water quality demands.

AMERICAN CAMPING CONVENTION 

MARCH 6th - 10th, 1962 


NEW YORK, NEW YORK IS A WONDERFUL TOWN . . . 

a wonderful place to gather together. Come to the American Camping Associa¬ 
tion National Convention March 6- 10th, 1962. for stimulating formal programme; 
come to exchange ideas informally with camp people from all parts of the United 
States and Canada; come, last but not least to enjoy our town. 

The Special Events Committee has interesting plans for you — a special 
meeting for those in attendance at the United Nations, a very special cookout 
at the Tavcrn-on-the-Grecn in Central Park. We hope that you will register 
in advance that we may have the pleasure of knowing how many of our friends 
from north of the border will be with us. 

The Hospitality Committee is arranging an attractive spot in the Statler- 
Hilton where you can rest your tired feet and talk with friends over a cup of 
coffee. On-the-town suppers are being arranged. You may choose from a 
variety of restaurants and cuisines. No worry about finding the place or getting 
a table, for a Hospitality Committee member will make arrangements and 
escort your group. 

You can ice skate at Rockefeller Center or in Central Park, attend the 
opera, and visit theatres on and off Broadway. You can take the subway to see 
Wall Street, and if you wish, lunch at Fraunces Tavern (Broadway and Pearl 
Street) where Washington said farewell to his officers. You may visit the New 
York Historical Society, the Museum of Natural History, and the Museum of 
the City of New York. Whatever your interests or hobbies are, you can follow 
them here. Plan to arrive early and stay late. 

Last but not least, you can take one of the most exciting sight-seeing trips 
in the world and absolutely the cheapest. If you lunch at Fraunces Tavern, go to 
Battery Park nearby and take the Staten Island Ferry for a nickel. From the 
deck of your boat, you will have a wonderful view of the skyline of lower 
Manhattan, the Statue of Liberty, and the Brooklyn Bridge. Of course, you 
will have to pay another nickel to get back to Manhattan, and you will have 
the whole panorama for the second time. No city can offer more for a dime.

THE SCRUB CLUB 

By Bruno Morawetz, 

Director, 

Camp Ponacka 

lowarcl tlu* end ol each camp period 
we usually have “turn-about day*' 
when each person becomes someone 
else. Some years ago a boy from In¬ 
diana was chosen to change places 
with my wife. Archie came to our 
cabin to trade clothes but my wife 
found it almost impossible to don his 
green shirt, richly decorated with large 
Birds of Paradise. It was not the birds, 
but the odor which repelled her. I 
had noted that lie wore the same kind 
of shirt most ol the month and enquiry 
revealed that it was not the same kind, 
but the same shirt which he had worn 
since his arrival some three weeks 
before! 

This is likely to happen in any camp 
but more so in ours where boys are 
responsible for doing their own laun¬ 
dry. The institution now known as the 
“Scrub Club” began in a very natural 
way. Unlike most camps, Ponacka was 
never properly established, it just grew. 
The dozen boys who were its seedlings 
supplied all the needs of the camp 
operation. They washed dishes, dug 
garbage holes, supplied the wood for 
the kitchen stove. It was only natural 
that they would also wash their own 
clothes. 

An old black boiler was placed over 
a fire near the lake to constitute the 
hot water supply. The rules of con¬ 
servation were rigidly practised. The 
same tubful of hot water was used for 
the camper's hot bath and served a 
few minutes later for his performance 
on the scrub board. Soon, frills made 
their appearance. Some ambitious 
counsellor induced his boys to put a 



railing around the area and one morn¬ 
ing a painted sign appeared over the 
entrance to this area bearing the proud 
inscription “Scrub Club.” This desig¬ 
nation induced a special kind of snob¬ 
bishness in the club members, enforced 
by the realization that very few such 
clubs are in actual existence. This 
feeling of exclusiveness by no means 
decreased the drudgery of the actual 
laundry operation. 

I he other signs of pioneering grad¬ 
ually disintegrated in the face of 
pressures finding expression in phrases 
like “My friend goes to camp so and 
so and they don’t wash dishes or dig 
garbage holes”. In order to be com¬ 
pel itive we had to yield and do “what 
other camps do” but in this one case 
Ponacka held out against the tide. The 
location of the Scrub Club moved with 
the exigencies of the times. At first it 
was imperative that it be located near 
the lake, the only source of water. 
As the vigilance of the Department of 
Health increased and laundry opera¬ 
tions could no longer be performed 
around the lake, we made use of our 
new pressure system and moved well 
back into the woods. This had a 
great advantage, especially when show¬ 
ing visitors around the camp. It can 
easily be imagined what the “club” 


64 


Canadian Camping 



looks like after one cabin group 
finishes, let alone all 64 campers. The 
price of tolerable condition is eternal 
vigilance. Eight year old campers es¬ 
pecially, take no great interest in the 
well being of their socks (nor do they 
care whether their mating is legitimate 
or a common law co-existence on the 
feet of the same person). 

Supervision and instruction are as 
necessary here as on the waterfront. 
This dubious distinction falls on the 
shoulders of our longsuflfering C.I.T.’s. 
The use of a scrub board has to be 
explained, proportions of soap to water 
demonstrated and stern warnings must 
be issued never to mix red socks with 
white T-shirts. 

At one time even sheets were washed 
by the campers themselves. The results 
were devastating not only to the sheets 
but to our public relations with exas¬ 
perated mothers. It was an unforget¬ 
table experience to behold (and no 
doubt, to perform) the act of wringing 
out a well drenched flannelette sheet, 
especially by an eight year old. It did 
encourage the kind of co-operation so 
badly needed in the world. Four little 
hands screwing in oppposite directions 
were better in squeezing out the soapy 
water than two, but the dreadful 
thought remained that it had to be 
done again after rinsing. The indepen¬ 
dent types used a tree instead of a 
buddy. By wrapping the sheet around 
a young tree the sheet could be forced 
to surrender its surplus moisture. These 
were some of the considerations which 
led us to send sheets to the laundry. 

Washing may be bad, but drying is 
worse. Some primitive tribes step out 
of their winterclothes forgetting that 
they will be needed again next winter. 
Boys treat clothespegs in an identical 
manner. Without pegs, drying is a 
problem which is not too readily 
recognized. Clothes hang well over the 
lines while they are wet. That they 
behave in the wind like dandelion 


seeds is not always appreciated. For 
that reason, regular reminders are 
issued in the dining room, especially 
when storm clouds gather, to have the 
laundry lines cleared. Like so many 
other reminders they fall on deaf ears. 
For the city child milk comes from 
bottles, for the camper clothing comes 
from neat stacks in a drawer. The 
connection between clean clothes for 
tomorrow and the clothesline today is 
hard to establish. After all, what could 
be more uninteresting! 

There are many inconveniences in 
operating a scrub club and the ques¬ 
tion often arises “Is it worth it”? The 
easy way out is, no doubt, to send all 
clothing out. But certain values would 
be lost. With urban living few boys 
enjoy the advantages of being res¬ 
ponsible for regular chores and few 
boys appreciate the labour of their 
mothers. Philosophers have drawn a 
fruitful distinction between work and 
labour. Work is creative, labour re¬ 
petitive. A mother’s life is highly re¬ 
petitive and it will not hurt a boy’s 
appreciation if he experiences that 
aspect of her daily life. It also teaches 
him to take greater responsibility for 
his belongings, not to mention the 
ordinary bits of knowledge about 
shrinkage and the “running” of colours. 

It may be construed as a loss of 
valuable camp time, but since it occurs 
only two or three times a month this 
charge is not too serious. Very few 
campers have been heard complaining; 
they seem to accept it as part of life’s 
necessities. Like spanking, it is harder 
on us than on them. The seasoned 
campers have learned to live with it, 
they wear grey sweaters or other kinds 
of clothing which never show dirt. We 
can infallibly distinguish the seasoned 
from the inexperienced camper by the 
size of the laundry bag which lie 
carries up the hill to the Ponacka 
Scrub Club. 


Toronto , Canada , February 1962

First of n series 


WHY I DIRECT A CAMP 

Elmer F. Ott, 

Y.M.C.A. Camp Manito-wish, 
Boulder Junction, Wisconsin 


As a visitor walked into camp from 
the parking lot he met a twelve-year- 
old boy to whom he said, “If there is 
a counsellor about, I would like to 
talk to him”. 

“I am a counsellor, sir.” replied the 
boy. “What can I do for you?” 

“You, a counsellor? You are too 
young to be a counsellor!” 

“Oh no, sir. You see everyone in 
this camp is a counsellor to some boy 
younger than he. We are all coun¬ 
sellors to someone except the director’s 
baby. He’s the only one too young to 
be a counsellor.” 

This story demonstrates the philoso¬ 
phy behind the way I feel a good camp 
should be operated. When each mem¬ 
ber of the camp community assumes 
responsibility for a part of its success 
and for decision making, I feel I con¬ 
tribute to leadership training and to 
the understanding of the democratic 
way of life. 

In this atmosphere there is time for 
relaxation and creativity. There is time 
and opportunity for experimentation. 
I believe by creating these conditions 
I offer young men and women oppor¬ 
tunity for personal growth and maturity. 

To operate a camp in this fashion 
for over a quarter of a century is not 
without personal satisfaction. The re¬ 
ward of seeing a shy lad stand up to 
assume a positive leadership role among 
his fellows far overshadows the mone¬ 
tary recompense other professions offer. 


When a counsellor said of his camp¬ 
ing experience, “My whole outlook on 
life has changed. I am setting my 
sights a lot higher after finding I can 
really do a great many things I once 
doubted I could do,” I feel I have 
made an investment in the potential 
of youth. 

When a camper said, “If you had 
told me before I came to camp that 
hard work could be fun, that by work¬ 
ing beside another fellow I could 
develop a close friendship that would 
last a life time, I would have called 
you nuts. Now, I’ve got to admit you 
are right,” thus I felt I had contri¬ 
buted to the boys’ appreciation for 
work. 

The canoe trip where there is no 
place for the loafer more than any 
other activity teaches the respect for 
the dignity of hard work. One lad 
upon returning from such an ex¬ 
perience wrote these words: 

“In each canoe, but two men worked; 
The 3rd man sat at ease 
To be more fitting for the coming tasks. 
And when in time a man grew weak 
From constant strain of ann and back, 
This rested man would spell his friend 
And so trade work for rest.” 

When personal behaviour indicates 
lives have taken on new meaning and 
personal goals are set in terms of high 
human values, then operating a camp 
becomes indeed worthwhile. 

turn to page 72 


66 


Canadian Camping 



from page 57 

them the thrill of finding and exploring 
new areas. 

By 1912 campers had visited 106 
lakes. Here too a subtle incentive had 
been set up in the form of the Honor 
Roll. In order to have your name 
inscribed on it you had to have won a 
certain number of senior points for 
athletics and visited at least 50% of 
the known lakes. Since it was practi¬ 
cally everyone’s ambition to get his 
name on the Roll many of the trips 
were organized on a “lake getting” basis. 
To see a lake from a mountain ridge 
did not count, you had to be close 
enough to “spit-in-it.” This same, if 
somewhat inelegant tradition is still 
being followed, and if all the spittle 
so expended could be gathered in one 
place we’d probably have a new lake. 
This would bring the present total 
close to the 300 mark. 

— Influence Of Founder — 

This, then, is the camp of yesteryear. 
Unorganized, freetime activities with 
heavy accents on tripping. Except for 
the meal time “horns” there were no 
whistles, no bells and no programme. 
Every day was free time for all kinds 
of land and water sports or fishing 
but the boys loved it and somehow 
they all seemed to acquire the practical 
skills that would stand them in good 
stead in the years to come. Powter’s 
was the reflection of its founder, he 


took part in every activity and if he 
didn’t excel in all of them the boys 
respected his ability and the man him¬ 
self. He played with them but brooked 
no nonsense especially of a dangerous 
or destructive nature, and in language 
lie was adamant against profanity. If 
someone slipped out with a curse, C.B. 
would quietly remark “What have you 
got left to say when you’re really 
mad?” 

As I sit writing this piece a snow 
storm is raging outside. Dimly through 
the driving snow I can look across 
the bay to the camp with its brown 
painted buildings trimmed with yellow. 
Now there is a road into camp, elect¬ 
ricity, water and flush toilets. But the 
sandbank still stands just as it did in 
1905 when C.B. first saw it and chose 
the site. Far more clearly I see the many 
hundreds of boys who worked and 
played together during their summers 
at Powter’s. Soon the snow and ice 
will melt away and the 60th season of 
Camp will be in full swing. My son, 
also a Charles Barrett, will be the 
Camp Director and he and his staff 
will again be imparting the same skills 
as the original C.B. did so many years 
ago. And if the management is in its 
third generation, many of the campers 
will also be third generation. From 
my position in the middle I find it 
difficult to judge if the camp is 60 
years old or 60 years young. 


3n Jfllemortam 

Miss Wilda Watson, B.A. joined the staff of Camp Onawaw fifteen years 
ago and her interest grew continuously. She became an active member of the 
Ontario Camping Association, a visitor for the Standards Committee and also 
proof read the Canadian Camping Magazine. She was a member of the staff 
of Lambton Kingsway School for twenty-seven years. Her loss will be felt 
by both the teaching and the camping professions.

This second year of the course con¬ 
tinues much of the work of the previous 
year. The purposes and objectives of 
camping are continually interpreted 
and articulated for those people who 
are registered in the C.I.T. course. In 
addition, an introduction to human 
behaviour; to need; personality devel¬ 
opment; and those social influences 
which affect behaviour is begun. Rec¬ 
ognizing the age of this group no 
attempt is made to explore these par- 
ticuluar topics, intensively, but cer¬ 
tainly familiarization with the whole 
area of social development for young¬ 
sters is attempted. 

As was mentioned both courses offer 
opportunity for personal development 
and growth. Cabin and staff dis¬ 
cussions, as well as personal counsel, 
assist these candidates in self-realiza¬ 
tion and evaluation.

Leadership For Leaders 

Naturally the question of staff to 
handle such a course arises. Believing 
this programme to be of priority, our 
department selects and trains a staff 
whose task it is during our camping 
season, to conduct and supervise, as 
well as initially plan the curriculum 
for the courses. To fill these posts, 
our personnel committee selects persons 
of considerable capacity; of advanced 
maturity; and of high moral character. 
A Training Director and two assistants 
comprise the three man training team. 
In order to co-ordinate the efforts of 
the boys’ and girls’ teams for the 
department and to preserve a consis¬ 
tency in curriculum, in all three camps, 
one of the training directors assumes 
the responsibility of supervisor whose 
duties include the preparation of 
course material and the orientation of 
training personnel prior to camp. In 


68 


Canadian Camping 




addition to the actual conduct of the 
training courses, the training staff also 
serve as advisers for counsellors and 
department heads who will have super¬ 
vision of the C.I.T.’s on the job, so 
that the training technique is con¬ 
sistent throughout the camp. They 
also act as consultants for our three- 
day annual staff training course held 
during Easter school vacation. This 
course is the final stage of formal 
training for camp staff members and 
participation in it is mandatory for all 
of our programme staff. 

Following graduation from the 
Junior Leader course and subsequently 
from the C.I.T. course, participants 
are then candidates for staff positions 
within our camping department. These 
positions depend upon vacancies that 


are available and the suitability of the 
candidate for those vacancies. Needless 
to say we cannot use all of our grad¬ 
uates. Many of them find their way 
to other camps in this country and 
even beyond. They do so with our 
recommendation and assistance. Others 
will wait a year or two before return¬ 
ing to camp when vacancies occur on 
staffs. 

The courses and the entire training 
structure are not foolproof but we are 
constantly evaluating and revising the 
programme in order to maintain it as 
a dynamic and realistic feature in ser¬ 
ving the staff and leadership needs of 
our Y.M.C.A. Camping Department 
and indeed those of camping in 
general.

There are many programmes for an Indian Council, Here is one — 


INDIAN COUNCIL PROGRAMME 


By /. ]. Keith , 

Assistant Director, Junior Camp, 
Camp Nominingue, Que, 


Summer witnesses the return to life 
of Canadian camping, as camps of 
different types, varying philosophies 
and widely scattered aims, reopen for 
another season. No two camps may 
be considered alike. With this wide 
variety in programmes, it is noted that 
in the majority of cases one common 
bond exists between institutions. Most 
camps take pride in associating them¬ 
selves in some small way with their 
“Indian Forefathers'* through tribal 
divisions, forms of Indian lore and 
many other activities. The one item 
that the majority do use in their 
regular programme cycle is that which 
is popularly known as Indian Council 
Ring. 

The Indian Council Ring appears 
in many camps on a weekly basis, and 
it is no understatement when one 
claims that this programme, despite 
its regularity, is one of the most pop¬ 
ular from the camper’s point of view. 
Considering its popularity, we soon 
realize that this provides a “ready¬ 
made” audience which, each of us in 
the camping field should utilize in 
order to demonstrate certain camping 
skills and knowledge. 

Many Council Rings have as a 
regular feature the reading of the 
“tribal narrations”. At this point, the 
Chief Scribe reads a series of camp- 
centered articles. The bulk of these 
tend to be in the humorous vein, 
laughing at some aspect of camp life 
and certain items of gossip which tend 
to be amusing. At no time during these 
amusing readings should the writer 


and reader descend to ridiculing, or 
running the risk of hurting a camper 
by causing others to laugh at him in 
other than an amused but “take it or 
leave it” manner. 

Perhaps the most important section 
of the narrations occur in what might 
be described as the editorial. Here the 
reader discusses some serious camping 
topic with the object of aiding each 
and every camper, increasing his 
appreciation of some aspect of camp 
life, or any other of many possibilities. 
Such topics as water safety, good 
canoe trip habits, conservation, the 
reading of others’ experiences in the 
forests, characteristics of the good 
camper may be used successfully. The 
Chief Scribe has before him a listening 
and attentive audience, and he would 
be failing in his ta^k if he were not 
to make use of this opportunity to 
briefly discuss such items. 

While on the topic of Council Ring 
discussion, a brief word should be said 
about canoe trip reports and their 
value. Many camps are built as trip¬ 
ping camps and consider their main 
feature to be this activity. Campers 
arc encouraged to participate in trips 
and become good trippers. In Council 
Ring, considerable reference is made 
to those “chiefs and braves camping by 
other lakes”. Thus, at some time 
during the season it is only right that 
representatives of various canoe trip 
parties be given the opportunity to 
share their experiences with their 
fellow chiefs and braves. 


70 


Canadian Camping 


Perhaps the greatest sin of those 
who give canoe trip reports is the 
tendency to describe their trip chrono¬ 
logically from the moment of departure 
to the return from distant lakes. The 
type of report which ambles on in a 
“that morning we ate porridge, pan¬ 
cakes and toast at seven o’clock, 
washed our dishes, packed and de¬ 
parted from the campsite at nine. We 
paddled across Lake Abenakis in ten 
minutes and then portaged to the next 
lake in about fifteen minutes” manner 
is nothing more than a monotonous 
and unimaginative speech, wasting the 
time of both speaker and listener. We 
should remember that a captive audi¬ 
ence is in attendance and make this 
an opportunity to provide both amuse¬ 
ment and propaganda for the canoe 
trip programme. Each person giving 
such a talk should confine himself to 
the description of one, two, or maybe 
three highlights of the trip and these 
should be described vividly. The sight¬ 
ing of a deer, observing the beaver at 
work, some unusual incident that took 
place, or similar topics, should be dis¬ 
cussed. This is what the campers want 
to hear; they have no great desire to 
know the time or arrival at any one 
of twenty lakes. 

The Council Ring provides the 
prime opportunity to demonstrate in¬ 
dividual prowess. No other programme 
in camp is capable of focusing so much 
attention on individual feats of skill 
and strength as the challenge of the 
Council Ring. Here, within the group, 
each brave is able to participate at 
some time in one challenge or another. 
Many of these challenges will be of 
the humorous variety (cracker eating, 
penny finding, bread and jam eating, 
bucket racing, fast talking, etc.) but 
others will put necessary emphasis on 
strength (Indian arm wrestle, leg 
wrestle, pacldle holding, etc.) and 
camping skill (chopping, fire building, 
tent pitching, etc.). 


Again, the challenge portion of the 
Council Ring provides excellent oppor¬ 
tunity to place many key camping 
activities before the braves. If there 
is to be a chopping contest, one of 
the chiefs might give a demonstration 
of this skill, along with a brief 
description of proper care and hand¬ 
ling of the axe. Perhaps one or more 
Council Rings each summer could be 
devoted to campcraft demonstrations 
and there, before the captive audience, 
camping skills can be displayed in the 
manner of our “Indian forefathers”. 

As may be readily seen, Council 
Ring deservedly ranks high in camp 
programmes. One aspect, as yet un¬ 
touched but none the less important, 
which must be given great considera¬ 
tion, is the location of the Council 
Ring. In order that the proper atmos¬ 
phere may be obtained, it is wise to 
place the ring in a remote, wooded 
area of camp, away from the usual 
activity areas. Thus the “sacredness” 
and importance of the Council Ring 
becomes more emphasized by the in¬ 
frequent visits to this place. 

Being in a distant wooded area, long 
paths to and from the ring may be 
made. The braves should be impressed 
with the idea that one of the prime 
characteristics of the Indian was his 
ability to keep silent in the forest. 
Thus, if we are to emulate him, we 
too must remain silent as we walk 
along this path, and while in the 
Council Ring. Laughter at humorous 
incidents may be permitted, but cheer¬ 
ing and talking should be discouraged. 
Any acknowledging of winners, good 
reports and other Council Ring items 
should be done with a vigorous “how, 
how”. Silence helps the brave prepare 
himself by becoming more aware of 
what he sees about him as he goes to 
the Council Ring. Thus, he is better 
able to absorb and enjoy the pro¬ 
gramme.

fro vi page 71 

The Council Ring is, therefore, a 
key part of many camp programmes. 
It provides an excellent opportunity to 
place the various aims and objectives 
of the camp before the campers when 
they are in a most receptive mood. 
Campcraft skills, nature lore, and 
other related activities are best placed 
before the entire group at this time. 
Above all, Council Ring provides the 
time and place for what amounts to a 
general summing up of camp, camp 
life, and what camp stands for in the 
eyes of each and every camper. 

—• 


from page 66 

Much of the school and recreational 
life of today’s youth is highly com¬ 
petitive, therefore, I believe in de¬ 
emphasizing this aspect in camp. To 
see boys and girls take part in camp 
life for the intrinsic value of the 
activity itself rather for the joy of 
beating the other fellow is one of the 
real rewards I find in camping. 

There is satisfaction in helping youth 
develop a personal philosophy of life. 
Camp offers opportunity for a great 
many enriching experiences. The close 
intimate contact with peers forces the 
weighing of ideas and ideals different 
from the camper’s own. Here there is 
necessity to express convictions and to 
formulate beliefs. The need for effort 
expended to carry one’s share of the 
community work load, the study of the 
cause of personal behaviour upon 
others and the building of a com¬ 
munity of one’s own choosing all make 
for personal growth. 

This growth comes about in many 
as a spiritual experience in which the 
individual secs himself as a brother of 
all mankind, a person of worth in the 
sight of God and man. Each becomes 
a counsellor of self and others. This is 
the paramount reason, I believe, I 
direct a camp. 

—•
